title: Closing a single-copy gap to the Holevo bound with two-copy measurements
abstract: The Holevo Cramér-Rao bound sets the asymptotically attainable precision of quantum multiparameter estimation, but its attainability with finite quantum state copies remains unresolved in general. While a gap between the single-copy optimum and the Holevo bound persists at any finite copy number for two-parameter estimation models, the higher-parameter case has remained open. Here we disprove universal finite-copy gap persistence beyond two parameters by constructing a three-parameter rank-two model whose Holevo bound is unattainable with one copy but attained exactly with two. We further prove finite-copy persistence for full-rank models with any number of parameters. We then experimentally implement the two-copy collective measurement for the constructed model using superconducting qubits. We observe a two-copy estimation error below the single-copy and separate-measurement bounds determined from state tomography. By introducing controlled depolarization, we show that this precision advantage persists over a finite noise range. Our results connect the attainability of ultimate quantum precision to the structure of the multiparameter estimation model and the resources available for collective measurements.
summary: This paper tackles the fundamental question of how close finite quantum measurements can get to the ultimate theoretical precision limit (the Holevo bound). By constructing a specific, rank-deficient model, the authors prove that the gap between single-copy and two-copy estimates can close. They validate this theoretically derived advantage experimentally using superconducting qubits, showing the two-copy measurement significantly outperforms single-copy estimates even when noise is present.
main_problem: The paper investigates the finite-copy gap in quantum multi-parameter estimation, specifically comparing the single-copy optimum bound to the ultimate Holevo bound.
main_result: The authors disprove the universal persistence of this gap beyond two parameters by constructing a rank-deficient three-parameter model where the two-copy measurement achieves the Holevo bound. Experimentally, they demonstrate a two-copy advantage over single-copy bounds using superconducting qubits.
method: The study combines theoretical proofs regarding model rank deficiency with experimental implementation using superconducting transmon qubits to measure estimation costs under controlled noise.
model_or_system: The theoretical model is a three-parameter, rank-two quantum estimation model. Experimentally, the platform uses superconducting transmon qubits on an IBM processor, implementing a hybrid two-transmon protocol.
key_observables: The primary observables are the estimation error costs: the single-copy optimum ($C^{(1)}_{opt}$), the two-copy measurement cost ($C^{(2)}_{exp}$), and the theoretical Holevo bound ($CH$).
important_parameters: The key parameters include the number of parameters (three), the number of copies (two), and the injected depolarizing noise strength ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical analysis distinguishes between rank-deficient and full-rank models, where rank deficiency is shown to be necessary for the gap closure. Experimentally, the analysis relies on readout error mitigation techniques.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the measured two-copy cost below the single-copy and Holevo bounds, showing the advantage persists over a finite noise range. Figure S2 tracks the difference between the single-copy lower bound and measured costs across various injected noise levels.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by constructing a specific rank-deficient model to close the gap at two copies. It then proves that full-rank models maintain the gap for any finite copy number. The latter part details the experimental realization on superconducting qubits, measuring the advantage and its robustness against controlled depolarization.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the fundamental limits of quantum measurement precision, providing concrete physical examples (superconducting qubits) where collective measurements can surpass single-shot estimates, linking fundamental theory (model rank) to experimental capability.
